tei:titleStmt.tei:title: מַֽהֲרוּ כׇּל־שָׁרִים
Maharu Kol Sharim — a pizmon on the parting of the Sea of Reeds with stanzas added in YU MS 1126

tei:div.tei:head: Maharu Kol Sharim — a pizmon on the parting of the Sea of Reeds with stanzas added in YU MS 1126

tei:lg.tei:l: Make haste, all singers, and in great potency and might!
Orate a song to the Deity, Rock, dwelling in my heights!
Split was the Reed Sea; and in its midst the Deity’s folk.
Entitled as “children,” they passed in my myriads!
I will entreat; await the Merciful;
good cheering I grant to the Compassionate;
offering and praise
and entreaty to the God of faith.
Behold, my Parent is awake, unsleeping,
and my tongue, lest I give sleep!
Deity, highest of the high,
we will raise faith to the merciful Deity!
Goodness They give me. I will entreat,
I will repeat Torah and give
daily and nightly song and cheer
to the God of faith.
So, those who hope for good, give thanks for the Deity
who will yet again, once more, gather up my children.
Thus Moses and the children of Israel would sing
this song to the Cause. (Exodus 15:1)

tei:note.tei:p: In the text recited in the Seattle and Istanbul communities, written הוֹן “riches.” However, all manuscripts and earlier printings agree on the rarer word אוֹן “potency,” which makes more sense in context.

Found incorporated in YU MS. 1126. These three stanzas are not found in the text recited in the Seattle and Istanbul communities, and in the parallel Shirei Yisrael b-Erets ha-Qedem nusaḥ they are treated as an optional insertion. Considering their near-complete lack of any rhyme scheme whatsoever, their form could almost be considered akin to blank verse, only clearly readable as poetry due to the meter and alliteration. They also interrupt the acrostic, which suggests they may not be original.

Wherever the Shirei Yisrael b-Eretz ha-Qedem has amen, YU MS. 1126 has omen. This word, here translated as “faith,” is likely a scribal error (and suggests that whichever scribe copied it down pronounced qamatz as a rounded vowel, in the manner of Ashkenazim, Temanim, and Persians.)

As found in the text recited in the Seattle and Istanbul communities, and (with the minor variation of a missing article prefix) the Shirei Yisrael b-Eretz ha-Qedem. YU MS. 1126 reads הוּא אֵל “for They are the Deity.”
Rearranged in YU MS. 1126 to יוֹסִיף שֵׁנִית הוּא “Yet again, once more They will”
In YU MS. 1126, בָּנָיו “Their children,” which is likely a mistaken hypercorrection to avoid switching to first-person for God, as it does not work with the rhyme scheme.
